questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: I wanted to do something different than just studying in Denmark and to try and live abroad and become a local in a new place.

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go where there were beautiful nature close by the university, interesting courses taught in English, not too many other students from KU and not too big a city.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Just go! You wont regret it :)

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. They had good emails with information and an online orientation program before arrival.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There were a lot of orientation events for international students on campus arrranged by volunteering students. It was very helpful, informative and fun events and you got to meet other exchange students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found something pretty fast through facebook groups, but have heard from others who really struggled finding something. And it depends on how much you are willing to pay as well.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Use facebook groups and make a post yourself about looking for housing, and do it earlier than everybody else. Dont just answer other peoples posts who are searching for renters.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
UVIC doesnt have enough housing so they cant guarantee housing for exchange students, so you can pay a fee to be in a draw, but its not sure you are gonna get the housing anyways. And its expensive (more than what you can find yourself) and there is a chance you are gonna live with all the first year canadian students (18 year old) and without a kitchen.

Find something close to campus, because that is where you are gonna be spending most of your time and where most other students live!

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
First you have to make sure you live up to all prerequisites and fill out and send in the aplications for courses with prerequisites.
Then you get a time slot, which is the same for every exchange student, to register for classes. Beforehand it is a good idea to have made a list with all the classes you want (and no overlapping classes), because then you can just click on one button and register for all the classes on that list at the same time.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You get a mail you can write to if you have problems with getting into one class or something.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all classes I wanted. No classes were full when I had to register, so dont stress too much about that.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Send in prerequisite applications for too many courses, and register for too many courses because then you can try them out in the first weeks and just drop the boring courses. You are probably gonna find at least one class very boring in the first week so its a good idea to have back ups, and therefore have already applied to fulfill prerequisites so you easily can register for the course or already have registered for it so it hasnt filled up.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took one second year course and 3 third year courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It is kinda the same with some courses with only big lectures for hundreds of students, others with smaller class lectures (30 students), and some with class lectures and then class labs or class tutorials (15 students). There is more work during the term, which counts towards the final grade, and some courses have mandatory attendance and weekly hand-ins of notes or weekly quizzes on the curriculum (i managed to avoid that in my courses though).

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
AE303A Introduction to ceramics wheel and hand techniques
EOS 350 Understanding the oceans
GEOG 252 Introduction to coastal geography
GEOG 376 Process Geomorphology

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
The ceramics course was really fun and a nice way to have less academic. It takes a lot of work though, but I would say it is worth it anyways.
The Process Geomorphology was the best course I have had ever. It was so interesting and a nice mix of lectures and interesting labs. I had to fight to get it because I didnt fully live up to the prerequisites, but I talked to the professor when I got to UVIC and after sending in a lot of documents it worked out.
Understanding the oceans starts out as a lot of repetition for a geographer student having had GGS, but then it changes and is actually a really nice course about specific problems in the ocean and sometimes a more thorough explanation of stuff than GGS.
The coastal geography is not really recommendable. The teacher was very boring, but at the whole grade was only made from easy assignments, so it meant that I had one less exam in december which gave me more time to travel.

Food DKK per month *

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: A mandatory health insurance and bus pass from UVIC, but then you could go to the Uni doctors and you could travel as much on the bus as you want to (you can get out of the bus pass if maybe you have a bike and are not planning on using the bus too much but the health insurance is mandatory).

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
The phone plans are very expensive in Canada. Fresh fruits and vegetables are more expensive than in DK.
It is possible to find cheaper housing, but I wanted to live close to campus and didnt want to spend to much time searching for other options.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: They have sooo many different clubs and organisations you can join. Sport clubs with all kind of sport you can imagine, organisations for every subject you can study, and other clubs with all kind of stuff you cant even imagine (a caving club, a fencing club, a pickles club...)

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
The caving club, it was such a fun and different activity I would never have done in DK. The people in the club are really nice and the caving trips were really fun. 
The climbing club, you can very cheap go to the climbing gym once a week and get all equipment and climb!
The outdoor clubs, the surfing club, the whitewater rafting sometimes make trips in the weekends, where you can go with other students and get to see a part of the island, try a fun activity and meet some fellow students (or bring your own friends).

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I would recommend you to, other than joining a club and going on a trip with them, to go on as many trips you can with your own friends in the weekends and holidays. See Tofino, Strathcona, Soothe, Vancouver, Whistler, Seattle, Banff, and so on. It makes the whole exchange experience so much more worth it, when you get to experience so much!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. Canada is not that different from Denmark, just a bit more americanized.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Try to talk to local students in your class or in clubs. Or if you live with canadians.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: It is not that easy to really become friends with canadians. They have their own friends, you are only there for half a year. It is easier to become friends with other exchange students.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: They are so nice. Everybody says thank you to the busdriver when they get off, the hold the door for you, they want to help you all the time.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Go to as many orientation events as you can the first week, that is where you meet other exchange students and make friends.
Go on trips and explore the island (and the main land) as often as you can!
Try to talk to canadian students in your class and in clubs, it is nice to come home and actually have gotten to know some canadians as well (and not only other europeans) :)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Dont hesitate to write to somebody from uvic if you have any questions, they are very helpful

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: All my friends I got and all the trips we went on!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
It is hard to actually become real friends with canadians and not just become acquaintanced. 
It is hard to start over and make new friends, and to become really close to people in only four months. But just give all you've got, give it time and enjoy it anyways.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
